questions.question_stem: A Fabric user presents a certificate issued by a known certificate authority, but the channel still rejects the user's proposal signature. Which explanation best fits the Hyperledger Fabric CA vs MSP distinction?
questions.correct_answer: The CA may have issued the credential, but the MSP and channel policies decide whether that identity and role count for this channel.
incorrect_answers: The CA may have issued the credential, but the orderer decides whether that user has a business role in channel chaincode policy.
The CA may have bound the public key, but committing peers decide channel membership only after MVCC validation completes.
The CA may have registered the identity, but chaincode lifecycle approval decides which clients can sign channel proposals.
questions.explanation: The lesson separates credential issuance from trust interpretation. CAs issue identities, while MSPs define which roots, roles, and signatures are recognized in local or channel policy contexts.

questions.question_stem: A client invokes chaincode in Fabric. Which sequence best captures what happens before a valid write reaches world state?
questions.correct_answer: Endorsing peers simulate and sign matching read-write sets, orderers sequence the transaction, then committing peers validate policy and MVCC before updating state.
incorrect_answers: Endorsing peers order the proposal into a block, committing peers simulate the chaincode, then orderers validate policy and MVCC before state changes.
Client gateways simulate and sign read-write sets, orderers validate endorsement policy, then committing peers append blocks before checking versions.
Endorsing peers simulate the proposal and update world state, orderers package the block, then peers check signatures only after commit events fire.
questions.explanation: Fabric's execute-order-validate path separates simulation, sequencing, and commit-time validation. Execution by an endorser is not the same as a committed world-state update.

questions.question_stem: A transaction appears in a block produced by the ordering service. A student says this proves the orderer accepted the transaction as business-valid. What is the best correction?
questions.correct_answer: Orderers establish a shared sequence; committing peers later determine validity using endorsement policy and state-version checks.
incorrect_answers: Orderers check endorsement signatures before sequencing; committing peers later only append the ordered block and refresh the state cache.
Orderers evaluate chaincode results for business validity; committing peers later repeat the same checks before updating world state.
Orderers decide whether each transaction is valid for the channel; committing peers later use gossip to distribute final state across peers.
questions.explanation: The lesson emphasizes that ordering is not business validation. An ordered transaction can still be marked invalid during peer validation and fail to update world state.

questions.question_stem: Two clients read the same asset version and both receive valid endorsements for different updates. One update commits first. What should happen to the later transaction if it reaches validation with the old read version?
questions.correct_answer: It should be marked invalid by MVCC validation because the read-set version no longer matches current world state.
incorrect_answers: It should be re-endorsed by the committing peer because validation can refresh the stale read-set version.
It should wait for the earlier block to propagate because gossip resolves version conflicts before commit.
It should commit after the first update because separate endorsements prove both clients approved writes.
questions.explanation: Committing peers check state-version assumptions during validation. A stale read set can be endorsed and ordered but still fail at commit time without changing world state.

questions.question_stem: A chaincode function includes the local system clock in the asset value it writes. Required endorsers simulate the proposal at slightly different times and produce different read-write sets. Why is Fabric right to reject the endorsement result?
questions.correct_answer: Matching endorsements require deterministic execution; disagreement signals that peers did not endorse the same proposed state change.
incorrect_answers: Matching endorsements require clock-aligned simulation; disagreement shows the proposal should be resequenced by the ordering service first.
Matching endorsements require the orderer to compare simulation outputs; disagreement shows consensus must execute the chaincode first.
Matching endorsements require committing peers to merge different write sets; disagreement shows MVCC should choose the latest simulated value.
questions.explanation: Deterministic chaincode matters because endorsers independently simulate the same proposal. Non-determinism can create mismatched read-write sets, and rejection preserves safety.

questions.question_stem: A consortium changes an endorsement policy from requiring either Bank A or Bank B to requiring both. What tradeoff should they expect?
questions.correct_answer: Greater multi-party assurance, but more latency and a higher chance that an unavailable or mismatching endorser blocks legitimate transactions.
incorrect_answers: Lower endorsement latency, but weaker multi-party assurance because either organization can still approve without the other bank's signature.
Greater ordering finality, but a higher chance that stale read versions overwrite each other during commit validation across channel peers later.
Stronger channel confidentiality, but more lifecycle governance because private data must move to a separate channel for every invoke.
questions.explanation: Endorsement policies encode trust logic. Requiring more endorsers can better match business approval requirements, but it increases coordination costs and availability sensitivity.

questions.question_stem: Several organizations share a channel, but only two should see a sensitive price field while everyone should still be able to verify that the transaction was anchored to the channel. Which Fabric mechanism best fits?
questions.correct_answer: Use a private data collection so authorized peers receive plaintext while the channel retains hash evidence for integrity.
incorrect_answers: Create a separate two-party channel and let the original channel verify the same price hash through configuration updates alone.
Use channel membership policies to hide plaintext from selected peers while the common ledger still stores the price hash for them.
Store the plaintext only in chaincode state and rely on endorsement signatures to reveal the hash to other channel peers securely.
questions.explanation: The lesson contrasts channels with private data collections. Collections are useful when a subset needs plaintext access but the broader channel should retain integrity evidence through hashes.

questions.question_stem: A developer has installed a chaincode package on one organization's peers, but normal application invokes fail because the channel has not accepted the definition. What concept explains the failure?
questions.correct_answer: Chaincode lifecycle is channel governance: organizations must approve and commit a definition before the contract version and policy are usable.
incorrect_answers: Endorsement policy is transaction approval: peers must collect enough signatures before an installed package can be referenced on the channel.
Channel MSP is identity governance: certificate roots must be updated before a peer can run any installed chaincode package on a channel.
Ordering service is block governance: orderers must install the package before they can include invokes in channel blocks and validate definitions.
questions.explanation: The lesson treats lifecycle as separate from ordinary business transactions. Installation alone is not equivalent to channel-level approval and commit of the chaincode definition.

questions.question_stem: An auditor can see a transaction in the block history, but a current query shows that the asset value never changed. Which interpretation best fits Fabric's ledger model?
questions.correct_answer: The transaction may be recorded in the immutable block log but marked invalid, so it does not affect the current world state.
incorrect_answers: The transaction may have reached endorsement but not ordering, so block history is showing a pending proposal response.
The transaction may be private data, so world state hides valid writes while the block log shows every plaintext value to auditors.
The transaction may have committed on another channel, so current queries on this channel reconcile through gossip later across peers.
questions.explanation: Fabric keeps a durable block log for audit while world state is a query-friendly current snapshot derived from valid transactions. Invalid block entries do not change current state.

questions.question_stem: A transaction never appears in any block, and monitoring shows the ordering service cannot make progress. Which failure category is most likely?
questions.correct_answer: A liveness failure in ordering, because the system is not producing the shared sequence needed before peer validation and commit.
incorrect_answers: A post-order MVCC conflict, because committing peers are rejecting a stale read set after the transaction is already in a block.
A pre-order endorsement failure, because peers produced mismatched read-write sets before the client could submit the envelope for ordering.
A gossip catch-up delay, because peers are missing block distribution after the orderer has already produced a block for the channel.
questions.explanation: The lesson distinguishes pre-order rejection, post-order invalidation, and ordering liveness stalls. If no block appears because ordering cannot progress, the symptom points to the ordering layer.

questions.question_stem: In Hyperledger Fabric, why is a cryptographically valid X.509 certificate not enough by itself to authorize an action on a channel?
questions.correct_answer: The relevant MSP and channel policies must recognize the issuing trust roots, identity attributes, role, and scope for that action.
incorrect_answers: The certificate proves a public key binding, but the ordering service alone decides whether that role is accepted on the channel.
The certificate must be included in the ledger first, so committing peers can derive channel permissions from world-state queries at commit.
The certificate is checked only after chaincode execution, so authorization depends mainly on the smart contract asset rules.
questions.explanation: The reading emphasizes that CAs bind identities to keys, but MSPs and policies turn verifiable identities into recognized permissions within local and channel scopes.

questions.question_stem: A peer was temporarily partitioned from the ordering service and missed several blocks, but it remains a valid channel member. What helps it catch up?
questions.correct_answer: Gossip lets channel peers disseminate signed ledger data so a lagging peer can pull missing blocks from peers that have them.
incorrect_answers: Raft lets endorsing peers resequence missed transactions so the peer can rebuild blocks from proposal responses later.
MSPs let the channel issue new credentials so the peer can recompute missing blocks from signed proposal responses and endorsements.
Lifecycle lets the peer reinstall chaincode packages so it can rebuild missed blocks from current world state after restart.
questions.explanation: The reading adds gossip as an operational synchronization mechanism. Signed peer-to-peer dissemination helps peers discover membership and recover ledger data after delays or partitions.

questions.question_stem: A Fabric channel uses a Raft-based ordering service. A majority of its consenters are unavailable. What consequence best follows from how Raft operates in this setting?
questions.correct_answer: Ordering for that channel stalls because Raft needs quorum to commit new ordered logs, even though existing block positions remain final.
incorrect_answers: Validation stalls because peers need a quorum of endorsers to mark ordered transactions valid, while old blocks stay readable.
Identity changes fail because channel MSPs need the Raft leader to issue certificates, while existing user signatures remain final for old blocks.
Execution stops because endorsing peers wait for orderers before simulating proposals, while previous world-state values remain durable.
questions.explanation: The reading frames Raft as crash-fault-tolerant deterministic ordering with a majority quorum. Loss of quorum is a liveness boundary for new ordering, not a rewrite of already fixed ledger positions.
